title: Are species occurrence data usable for quantifying biodiversity dynamics associated with land‐cover changes at a regional scale?
content:
We combine CORINE Land Cover data and GBIF Occurrence Records to model how species occurrence data varies as land-cover changes. We found that the impacts of change on the number of species occurrence records differed among land-cover change types. We conclude that whilst this approach poses significant challenges, it can still facilitate the assessment of land-use change impacts on biodiversity.


Abstract

Land-use and land-cover changes (LULCC) pose one of the greatest threats to biodiversity worldwide, impacting all dimensions of biodiversity in complex and multifaceted ways. However, impacts of LULCCs have mostly been assessed locally, over short temporal scales and with a taxonomically restricted focus.

The development of remote sensing technologies as well as the popularisation of citizen science and participatory monitoring programmes allows easy access to broad land-cover and biodiversity data. The integration of remotely sensed LULCC and species occurrence records now provides the potential for assessments of impacts across broader spatial, temporal and taxonomic scales. However, our understanding of the overlap between the collection of biodiversity data and areas of land-cover change as well as the feasibility of integration of the two data types is limited.

Here, we used Norway as an example of a country with a rich history of land-use changes and high abundance of species occurrence records to investigate the potential for integration of these data sources to address land-use impacts on biodiversity. We used CORINE Land Cover to map land-cover changes at a national scale since 2000 and species occurrence records from GBIF. We used a mixed modelling approach to model the relationship between land-cover changes, time and the availability of species occurrence records across Norway.

We found that the number of species occurrence records increases through time. We also found that some land-cover changes are associated with declines in the number of species occurrence records available.

Our results revealed a dynamic mosaic of land-cover changes across Norway in time and space, with impacts of changes on the number of occurrences recorded after a change differing between different land-cover change types.

Practical Implication: the integration of remotely sensed LULCC data and occurrence records poses significant challenges. However, by accounting for differing patterns in sampling of species occurrence data across changing land-covers, the approach can still provide a useful method for a comprehensive regional assessment of LULCC impacts across broader temporal scales.
